q: What is a programmer's model, as the course defines it?
choices: The published contract: state you can inspect and change, and its effects
A detailed description of the pipeline, bus matrix and silicon that runs your code
The full list of peripherals in the vendor's reference manual
The compiler's rules for turning C statements into instructions
why: It is a deliberately small, documented contract: the state software can name and its effects. The pipeline, bus matrix and silicon are the implementation it hides.

q: Which of these does the programmer's model deliberately leave out?
choices: The pipeline and the bus matrix
why: The model is registers, memory, peripheral registers, modes/stacks and exceptions. The pipeline, bus matrix and silicon are hidden implementation, named by none of your code.

q: How many parts does this chip's programmer's model have?
why: Registers, memory, peripheral registers, modes and stacks, exceptions. Everything in later lessons is an instance of one of the five.

q: Meeting a new peripheral, what is the first question the course wants you to ask?
choices: Which part of the model is this?
How fast can its clock run?
why: One model, many instances: every peripheral is the same shape wearing different names, so the first job is to place it in the model, then read its control/status/data registers.

q: How many core registers does the Cortex-M0+ have, and how wide are they?
why: Cortex-M has 16 × 32-bit registers (R0–R15). 32 × 8-bit is the AVR you came from; 32 × 32-bit is RISC-V.

q: R13 (SP) is one name for which two physical registers?
why: SP is one name, two registers: the main stack pointer MSP and the process stack pointer PSP. CONTROL bit 1 (SPSEL) picks which one Thread mode uses.

q: What is R14 for?
choices: It is LR, holding the return address
It is SP, the stack pointer
It is PC, the address of the next instruction to run
why: R14 = LR, the link register, holds the return address after bl. R13 is SP, R15 is PC; the exception number is in IPSR.

q: What happens when an instruction writes a new value into R15?
choices: The processor branches to that address
Nothing until the next interrupt arrives
The value is saved as a return address
The CPU faults: PC is read-only
why: R15 is the PC, an ordinary register: writing it is a branch. That is why pop {…, pc} works as a return.

q: Which registers carry function arguments in, the result out, and scratch values?
why: R0–R3 are arguments, result and scratch. R4–R12 hold locals kept out of memory; R13–R15 are SP, LR and PC.

q: xPSR is one word with three views. Which list names them correctly?
why: xPSR is read as APSR (flags N Z C V), EPSR (Thumb bit) and IPSR (exception number). CONTROL and PRIMASK are separate special registers.

q: Which bits of xPSR hold the N Z C V flags?
why: The APSR view keeps the flags at the very top, bits 31:28 (N=31, Z=30, C=29, V=28).

q: Where in xPSR is the Thumb bit T?
why: EPSR's T is bit 24. Bit 0 of code addresses is also called the Thumb bit, but in xPSR the T bit is 24; IPSR uses bits 5:0.

q: Which bits of xPSR hold the current exception number (IPSR)?
why: IPSR is the bottom of xPSR, bits 5:0. It is 0 in main() and the exception number inside a handler.

q: USART2 is IRQ 28. While USART2_IRQHandler runs, what does IPSR read?
why: IPSR holds the exception number, which is 16 + IRQ number: 16 + 28 = 44 = 0x2C. Reading back the bare IRQ number (28) forgets ARM's first 16 slots.

q: While ordinary code in main() runs, what does IPSR read?
why: IPSR is 0 in Thread mode code such as main(); it only holds a number while a handler runs.

q: xPSR reads 0x60000000 after a compare. Which flags are set?
why: 0x6 in the top nibble is 0110: bit 31 N=0, bit 30 Z=1, bit 29 C=1, bit 28 V=0.

q: xPSR reads 0x81000000. What does that tell you?
choices: N is set and the Thumb bit is set
Z is set and IPSR holds 1
V is set and the Thumb bit is clear
C is set and an exception is active
why: Top nibble 0x8 = 1000: only N (bit 31). 0x01000000 is bit 24, the T bit, which is always 1 here. Bits 5:0 are 0, so no exception is active.

q: What does setting PRIMASK bit 0 to 1 do?
why: PRIMASK bit 0 = 1 masks every configurable interrupt. SPSEL and nPRIV are CONTROL bits; the M0+ has no FPU.

q: What do the two used bits of CONTROL select?
choices: Bit 1 SPSEL picks Thread mode's stack; bit 0 nPRIV picks privilege
Bit 1 masks interrupts; bit 0 selects Thumb state
Bit 1 picks the system clock source; bit 0 enables the MPU's protection
Bit 1 selects Handler mode; bit 0 selects MSP
why: CONTROL bit 1 SPSEL chooses MSP or PSP for Thread mode; bit 0 nPRIV chooses privileged or not. The other thirty bits are reserved.

q: How does code read or write xPSR, PRIMASK and CONTROL?
choices: Only with mrs and msr; they have no address
With ldr/str at their address in 0xE000xxxx
With push and pop to the stack
Through CMSIS structs in the SCB block
why: The special registers have no number and no address, so ordinary loads and stores cannot reach them. Only mrs/msr can. The 0xE000xxxx region is the NVIC/SysTick/SCB, which are memory-mapped.

q: Can code on this Cortex-M0+ use BASEPRI to mask only low-priority interrupts?
choices: No: BASEPRI and FAULTMASK exist only on M3/M4
Yes: it is bit 1 of PRIMASK
Yes: BASEPRI is part of xPSR
why: The M0+ has PRIMASK only. BASEPRI and FAULTMASK are M3/M4 registers; assuming them is a common carry-over mistake.

q: What does a processor pay for having MORE working registers?
choices: More instruction bits to name one, more state to save per interrupt
More memory traffic, because the compiler must spill values to RAM more often
Slower loads and stores from every register
A larger stack for each function call
why: Too few registers and the compiler spills to memory; too many and every instruction needs more bits to name one and every interrupt has more state to save.

q: How does Cortex-M software reach a peripheral register?
choices: By ordinary ldr/str to an ordinary address
By special in/out instructions in a port space
Through a system call into the vendor library
Through mrs/msr, like the special registers
why: This chip uses memory-mapped I/O with no port space at all: peripherals sit at ordinary addresses and ordinary loads and stores reach them.

q: The AVR reached its I/O registers with IN and OUT. What is that style called?
why: A separate I/O address space reached by dedicated instructions is port-mapped, also called isolated, I/O. x86 in/out works the same way.

q: Which instruction does a Cortex-M use to set a GPIO output register?
choices: str, the same store used for a variable
out, as on the AVR and x86
why: With memory-mapped I/O there are no I/O instructions: the same str writes a variable or a peripheral. out belongs to port-mapped machines; sbi was the AVR's and the M0+ has none.

q: On this chip, what tells a GPIO register apart from a global variable?
choices: The instruction used to reach it
A tag bit in the pointer
Which bus instruction the compiler emits
why: Both are reached by the same ldr/str; the only difference is the address. That uniformity is both the gift and the trap.

q: Why can a stray pointer on this chip silently change a peripheral's behaviour?
choices: Peripherals are ordinary addresses and there is no MMU to stop it
The compiler ignores volatile on pointers
The MPU is always configured at reset to allow every access everywhere
Peripheral registers are cached in SRAM
why: Memory-mapped I/O plus one real address space with no MMU means any pointer can land on a peripheral; nothing raises a segmentation fault.

q: What does 'Harvard' mean as a memory organisation?
choices: Code and data live in separate address spaces
Code and data share one address space
Instructions are fetched over a cache
Data is stored big-endian, code little-endian
why: Harvard keeps code and data in separate address spaces, so the same address means two things. Von Neumann puts both in one space.

q: How does code on this chip read a const lookup table stored in flash?
choices: With LPM, after marking it PROGMEM
It must first be copied into SRAM
why: The Cortex-M address map is von Neumann: one space, so a const array in flash is read by the same ldr as anything else. PROGMEM/LPM existed only because the AVR is Harvard.

q: Which AVR keyword existed only because the AVR is a Harvard machine?
why: PROGMEM (with the LPM instruction) placed and read constants in program memory, a separate address space. It has no equivalent on Cortex-M.

q: Some Cortex-M cores fetch code and data over separate buses. Does that make their programmer's model Harvard?
choices: No: the address map stays single and code cannot tell
Yes: separate buses mean separate address spaces
Yes, but only for code stored in SRAM
Only when the instruction cache is enabled
why: Separate buses are an implementation choice for speed. The address map is still one space, so the model is von Neumann.

q: At what address does this chip's flash really live?
why: Flash is at 0x08000000. It is aliased to 0x00000000 at reset, but its real home is 0x08000000. SRAM is 0x20000000, ST's peripherals 0x40000000.

q: How does the CPU find the vector table 'at address zero' after reset?
choices: Flash at 0x08000000 is aliased to 0x00000000 at reset
A bootloader in system memory copies the vector table to address 0
SRAM starts at 0 and holds a copy of the table
The NVIC stores the table in its own registers
why: At reset the chip aliases flash to 0x00000000, so the two words at zero are the first two words of flash.

q: Where does SRAM start?
why: SRAM starts at 0x20000000: variables, stack and heap. Flash is 0x08000000 and ST's peripherals start at 0x40000000.

q: On the STM32C0, at which base do the GPIO ports sit?
why: ST's peripherals are mostly at 0x40000000, but on the STM32C0 GPIO is at 0x50000000 (GPIOA 0x50000000, GPIOB 0x50000400). 0xE000xxxx is ARM's.

q: The NVIC and SysTick are at 0xE000xxxx. Why does that matter when you look something up?
choices: They are ARM's, the same on every Cortex-M: open ARM's manual
They are ST's, so only ST's datasheet lists them
They are optional and absent on the M0+
They are mapped into flash, so the linker script must describe them
why: 0xE0000000 is ARM's private peripheral bus. ARM's Cortex-M Generic User Guide covers NVIC/SysTick; ST's reference manual covers everything else.

q: Which manual answers 'which pin does USART2 come out on'?
why: USART, GPIO, timers and pin muxing are ST's, so ST's reference manual answers. Interrupt priorities are ARM's NVIC, answered in ARM's guide.

q: Which of these blocks is ARM's, the same on every Cortex-M from any vendor?
why: ARM supplies NVIC, SysTick, SCB and MPU (core_cm0plus.h). ST supplies GPIO, USART, TIM, ADC and RCC (stm32c031xx.h).

q: SRAM is 12 KB starting at 0x20000000. What is the address just past its end (the top of RAM)?
why: 12 KB = 12 × 1024 = 12288 = 0x3000, so the top is 0x20003000, the initial stack pointer. 0xC000 would be 48 KB; 0x1200 confuses decimal 12 with hex.

q: Flash is 32 KB starting at 0x08000000. What is the first address past the end of flash?
why: 32 KB = 32768 = 0x8000, so flash ends just below 0x08008000. 0x20000 would be 128 KB.

q: A pointer holds 0x50000014. What is it pointing at?
choices: A GPIO register (ST's, on the STM32C0)
why: 0x50000000 is where the STM32C0's GPIO lives, so 0x50000014 is a register inside GPIOA. SRAM is 0x2…, flash 0x08…, NVIC 0xE000E100.

q: Which statement is true of a peripheral register but NOT of a RAM variable?
choices: Reading it can clear a flag or consume a byte
It is reached by an ordinary ldr
It has a fixed address in the memory map
why: Reading a register can have a side effect (clear a flag, pop a byte). Both are reached by ldr at a fixed address; that is not the difference.

q: Your code reads a status register twice in a row and gets two different values. What does that mean?
choices: Nothing wrong: hardware can change a register between reads
The bus is faulty or the clock is unstable, so reads are unreliable
The compiler reordered the two reads
A second task wrote the register in between
why: A register is a piece of hardware; reading it twice can give different values. A variable read twice gives the same value; a register need not.

q: Why must every access to a peripheral register happen exactly as written in the source?
choices: Reads and writes have side effects the compiler cannot see
Registers are slower than RAM, so a cached copy goes stale and corrupts them
Peripheral addresses change after each access
why: Writing makes something happen and reading can clear a flag, so caching, reordering or deleting accesses changes behaviour. That is what volatile forbids.

q: Every peripheral has three kinds of register. Which is written by hardware to report what happened?
why: Control registers are written by software to configure; status registers are written by hardware to report; data registers carry values in and out.

q: In the course's classification, which role does GPIO's IDR play?
choices: Status: it reports what the pins are
Data: it carries the payload out
why: The guide lists GPIO as MODER (control) / IDR (status) / ODR, BSRR (data). IDR reports pin levels, so it is a status register even though it 'holds input data'.

q: The USART has a register called ISR. What kind of register is it?
choices: A status register reporting events such as 'transmit buffer empty'
The address of the USART's interrupt service routine
A data register holding the byte most recently received on the line
A control register that enables interrupts
why: USART is CR1 (control) / ISR (status) / TDR, RDR (data). Here ISR means interrupt-and-status register, not a handler function.

q: For a timer, which pair are the data registers?
why: Timer: CR1, PSC, ARR are control; SR is status; CNT and CCR carry the values.

q: You configure a peripheral and its register reads back as zero. What should you suspect first?
choices: Its clock gate in RCC was never enabled
The pin multiplexer chose the wrong owner
The compiler optimised the write away
why: Every peripheral powers up unclocked: writes vanish and reads return 0. It is the most common first-week failure. A wrong pin mux leaves the registers working but the pin silent.

q: A peripheral works internally, the pin is electrically healthy, yet the pin carries no signal. Likely cause?
choices: The pin multiplexer gave the pin to the wrong owner
The peripheral's clock gate is off
The flash wait states are wrong
The vector table slot is empty
why: Each pin is shared between peripherals; choose the wrong owner and the pin carries nothing. A clock-gate fault would make the peripheral's registers read 0.

q: Which of the two gates gives you an error message when you forget to open it?
choices: Neither: both look like correct code that does nothing
The clock gate raises a HardFault
The pin mux sets an error flag in RCC that you can read back afterwards
Both: the compiler warns about each
why: Both gates fail silently: no fault, no warning, just correct code that does nothing. That is why you suspect them first.

q: What state is every peripheral's clock in at power-on?
choices: On, at the reset 12 MHz clock
Off for ARM blocks, on for ST blocks
why: Every peripheral powers up switched off. Opening its clock gate in RCC is your job.

q: A UART's baud-rate divisor must be computed from which clock?
why: A baud rate is a division of the peripheral's bus clock, not the CPU clock. Get the clock wrong and perfect code prints garbage.

q: Serial output is garbage but the transmit code is correct. Which cause fits this lesson?
choices: The clock the baud divisor assumed is not the real one
A missing volatile on the data register
The vector table holds even addresses, so the UART handler never runs
why: Garbage characters from perfect code mean a wrong clock or a divisor computed from the wrong clock.

q: How do you wait 1 ms on this chip?
choices: Count a known number of ticks
why: There is no operating system and no sleep(): a delay is a count of ticks of a known clock.

q: What does the core run at out of reset, and after the course's clock setup?
choices: 12 MHz (HSI48 ÷ 4), then 48 MHz with 1 flash wait state
48 MHz from reset, no wait states
8 MHz, then 64 MHz with 2 wait states
12 MHz, then 48 MHz with no wait states
why: Reset gives HSI48 ÷ 4 = 12 MHz. Raising to 48 MHz needs one flash wait state, set before the clock is raised.

q: On a desktop a bad pointer causes a segmentation fault. What hardware does that, and what does this chip have?
choices: An MMU; this chip has no MMU, only an optional MPU
An MPU; this chip has a full MMU
A cache; this chip uses flash wait states to do the same job instead
The NVIC; this chip uses SysTick instead
why: Desktops use an MMU for private virtual address spaces. This chip has two privilege levels, no MMU and optionally an MPU of permission rules over real addresses.

q: How does an MPU differ from an MMU?
choices: It applies permission rules to real addresses; no private virtual map
It translates virtual addresses for each task but cannot enforce any permissions
It only protects flash, never SRAM
It is the same thing under ARM's name
why: An MPU is a set of permission rules over the one real address space. An MMU gives each program a private virtual view of memory.

q: Where do main() and an interrupt handler run?
choices: main() in Thread mode, handlers in Handler mode
Both in Thread mode, on different stacks
main() in Handler mode, handlers in Thread mode
Both in Handler mode, at different priorities
why: Your main() runs in Thread mode; every interrupt runs in Handler mode. The processor switches without being asked.

q: Which stack does Handler mode use?
choices: The stack of the interrupted task
why: SPSEL only selects Thread mode's stack. Handler mode always uses MSP and is always privileged, so a fault handler still works when task code has wrecked its own stack.

q: How does an RTOS give each task its own stack?
choices: Tasks run in Thread mode on PSP, each with its own PSP value
Each task runs in Handler mode on MSP
The MPU allocates one stack per task automatically at task creation time
Every task shares MSP but with separate frames
why: An RTOS points PSP at each task's stack in Thread mode; handlers stay on MSP. Until the RTOS lesson, MSP serves everything.

q: CONTROL reads 0 after reset. What does that mean for Thread mode?
why: Both bits are 0 at reset: SPSEL = 0 (MSP) and nPRIV = 0 (privileged).

q: What is non-vectored interrupt dispatch?
choices: Every interrupt enters at one address and software asks who called
Each source's number indexes a table that holds the address of its handler
The CPU polls each peripheral in turn
Interrupts are queued and handled by main()
why: Non-vectored: one entry point, then software interrogates the hardware. Vectored: the source's number indexes a table and the hardware goes straight to the handler.

q: What does each slot of the Cortex-M vector table hold?
choices: A jump instruction to the handler
why: Cortex-M's table holds plain addresses. The AVR's slots hold jump instructions; x86's hold descriptors.

q: How does your USART2 handler get connected to the USART2 interrupt?
choices: Its name puts its address in the right slot of the table you build
You call an NVIC registration function for each handler during startup
The NVIC searches flash for a matching name
The linker script lists each handler by IRQ
why: There is no registration call. The table is built by your own code; a handler is connected because its address sits in the right slot.

q: In the vector table, what occupies the first 16 slots?
choices: ARM's exceptions: initial SP, reset and faults
Sixteen copies of the reset vector
The handlers for each GPIO pin
why: The first 16 slots are ARM's (slot 0 initial SP, slot 1 Reset_Handler, faults, SysTick…). Vendor interrupts start at slot 16.

q: USART2 is IRQ 28. Which slot of the vector table holds its handler's address?
why: Vendor interrupts start at 16, so IRQ 28 is in slot 16 + 28 = 44.

q: The vector table starts at 0x08000000. At which address is the vector for IRQ 3?
why: Slot 16 + 3 = 19, each slot 4 bytes: 19 × 4 = 76 = 0x4C. 0x0C forgets the 16 ARM slots; 0x13 forgets the × 4.

q: What do slots [0] and [1] of the vector table hold?
choices: The initial stack pointer and the Reset_Handler address
The NMI and HardFault handler addresses
The reset handler and the main() address
The table's size and its checksum
why: Slot 0 is the initial SP, slot 1 the reset vector. They are the only two words the hardware reads at reset.

q: Coming from AVR, you declare loop counters as uint8_t 'to save cycles'. On this chip that is
choices: often slower: the compiler must mask and shift to 8 bits
faster, since 8-bit ALU operations take fewer cycles than 32-bit ones
the same speed but saves a register
required, as registers are 8 bits wide
why: The word size is 32 bits; narrower types are emulated on top, so uint8_t is not cheaper and often costs extra masking.

q: What is natural alignment?
choices: An n-byte access uses an address divisible by n
Every access uses an address divisible by 32
Structs are padded to the cache line size
Data is stored most significant byte first
why: A bus moving 4 bytes at a time moves them between 4-byte boundaries, so an n-byte access wants an address divisible by n.

q: You cast a uint8_t receive buffer to uint32_t* and read a word at an odd offset. What happens on the M0+, and on an M3?
choices: M0+ HardFaults; an M3 performs it, more slowly
Both perform it, the M0+ more slowly
M0+ reads the aligned word below; an M3 faults
why: A Cortex-M0+ faults on any unaligned word access. M3/M4 perform ordinary unaligned loads and stores, just slower.

q: Which address is safe for a 32-bit ldr on a Cortex-M0+?
why: A word access needs an address divisible by 4: 0x104 = 260 is; 0x102, 0x101 and 0x107 are not and would HardFault.

q: Which 16-bit (uint16_t) access faults on a Cortex-M0+?
why: A halfword needs an even address; 0x…103 is odd. The others are all divisible by 2.

q: The word 0x12345678 is stored at address a. Which byte is at a?
why: Little-endian puts the least significant byte first: 0x78 at a, 0x56 at a+1, 0x34 at a+2, 0x12 at a+3.

q: The word 0xCAFE0142 is stored at 0x20000010. Which byte is at 0x20000012?
why: Little-endian bytes from 0x…10 are 42, 01, FE, CA, so offset 2 holds 0xFE. 0x01 would be the big-endian answer.

q: Memory from address a holds the bytes 10 32 54 76. What does a 32-bit ldr from a return?
why: The first byte is least significant, so the word reads back as 0x76543210.

q: Internet protocol headers use 'network byte order'. Which order is that?
choices: Big-endian, the opposite of this chip
Little-endian, the same as this chip
Whichever order the sender's CPU uses
why: Network byte order is big-endian (hence htonl()). Every STM32 is little-endian, so bytes from the network must be swapped.

q: Which three implementation details leak into code you must write?
choices: Pipelining, two buses (AHB/APB), slow flash wait states
The bus matrix, DMA, register renaming
why: The pipeline (PC reads ahead, taken branches cost), the AHB/APB buses with their own clock-enable registers, and flash wait states in FLASH->ACR.

q: Your clock code raises the core to 48 MHz and then sets the flash wait states. What is wrong?
choices: Wait states must be set first; the compiler cannot catch the order
Nothing: the order of the two register writes makes no difference at all
Wait states must be set after; the code is right
The compiler reorders them anyway, so it works
why: Flash cannot keep up at 48 MHz with zero wait states, so FLASH->ACR must be set first. The code compiles identically either way; only one order works.

q: What visible effect does pipelining have?
choices: The PC reads ahead, and a taken branch costs extra cycles
Every instruction takes exactly one cycle
Interrupts must wait for the pipeline to empty
Loads return the data from the previous instruction because of the overlap
why: Overlapping fetch, decode and execute means the PC reads ahead of the executing instruction, and a taken branch throws away work already started.

q: Why does a 32 KB microcontroller use flash wait states instead of a cache?
choices: It cannot spend the transistors on a cache
Caches do not work with Thumb code
Wait states are faster than a cache
Flash on this chip is as fast as the core
why: The processor–memory speed gap: large machines answer it with caches; a small part answers with wait states and a prefetch buffer.

q: GPIO and DMA hang off the fast bus; USART and timers off the slow one. Which pair?
why: AHB is the fast bus (GPIO, DMA, RCC) with RCC->AHBENR; APB is slow (USART, SPI, I2C, TIM, ADC) with RCC->APBENR1. Each has its own clock-enable register.
